title: AI in the Classroom: Why Has the Light Turned to Amber? https://educhatter.wordpress.com/2026/09/26/ai-in-the-classroom-why-has-the-light-turned-to-amber/
author: Paul W. Bennett
summary: Paul W. Bennett questions New Brunswick's decision to bring AI into its curriculum from kindergarten to Grade 12, just as New York City and Los Angeles move to ban it and the PISA 2025 results arrive. He notes that the province's own district superintendent compares resisting AI to holding back the Bay of Fundy's tides, while the same province tries to limit phones for younger children. Bennett cites a Fordham Institute report on illicit tech use and AI cheating, Jared Cooney Horvath's The Digital Delusion, and a new MIT report to argue that AI removes the productive struggle that builds intelligence and confidence. He reports that OECD analysis found frequent AI users scoring about 27 points below non-users on PISA science, while New Brunswick finished last among Canadian provinces. He closes with Daniel Willingham's advice that students should use AI only for things they already know well, and calls for a pause pending risk assessment.
points: New Brunswick is the first Canadian province to integrate AI across K-12, in tension with its own attempts to limit exposure of younger children to devices.
A Fordham report finds high rates of illicit tech use, with 26 percent of students using AI to cheat on tests or quizzes.
Critics argue that unsupervised AI use removes the productive struggle that builds cognitive capacity, which is the core purpose of school.
OECD data reported in the piece link frequent AI use for schoolwork to substantially lower PISA scores, which makes the province's weak results a concern.
Bennett recommends Willingham's rule that students use AI only for things they already know well and urges a pause for a proper risk assessment.
quotes: New Brunswick is incorporating AI into its school curriculum from kindergarten to Grade 12. It was, CBC News reported, the first province in Canada to do so.

One of its champions, N.B. Anglo East District superintendent Randolph MacLean maintains that trying to keep artificial intelligence out of New Brunswick schools is tantamount to “trying to hold back the Bay of Fundy’s tides
76 percent of students report some sort of illicit tech use at school, often on school-provided Chromebooks or iPads.

Unsupervised A.I. use, according to Cooney-Horvath and his allies, is essentially undermining a young person’s cognitive learning and development. It takes away the struggle necessary to grow both intelligence and confidence.
Students who use AI for schoolwork, the OECD Office reported, underperform those who don’t by a significant amount.

Fifteen-year-old Students from New Brunswick performed abysmally on PISA 2025, finishing with a 463, last among Canada’s provinces and territories. Why, then, would New Brunswick be going ‘gung-ho’ for AI in classrooms?
The best advice given, so far, is to handle with care and it comes from leading cognitive psychologist Daniel Willingham: “ Students should only use AI for things they already know well.

The new technology packs a one-two punch. In the first instance, screens and social media make people dumber by diminishing our attention span, while, at the same time, AI makes it easier to be stupid by doing our thinking for us.
